attributes.number: About 250 ethnic groups. Cameroon likes to call itself Africa in miniature.
attributes.five_groups: Often grouped into five regional-cultural divisions: western highlanders or Grassfielders (Bamileke, Bamoun, Tikar), about 38%; southern tropical forest peoples (Ewondo, Bulu and Fang, who are Beti subgroups, plus Maka and Baka), about 18%; coastal tropical forest peoples (Bassa, Duala and others), about 12%; the predominantly Muslim peoples of the Sahel and central highlands (Fulani), about 14%; and the Kirdi, about 18%. These shares are older estimates.
attributes.world_factbook_categories: A 2022 estimate reported by EBSCO gives: Bamileke-Bamu 22.2%, Beti/Bassa/Mbam 13.1%, Biu-Mandara 16.4%, Arab-Choa/Hausa/Kanuri 13.5%, Adamawa-Ubangi 9.8%, Grassfields 9.9%, Kako/Meka/Pygmy 2.3%, Cotier/Ngoe/Oroko 4.6% and Southwestern Bantu 4.3%.
attributes.caution: Estimates differ between sources and years, and none comes from a recent census.

source.citation: WorldAtlas, Ethnic groups of Cameroon, and GlobalSecurity.org, Cameroon people. Compiled for this collection and not yet reviewed by a second person.

attributes.home: The western highlands, in the West and Northwest regions.
attributes.languages: Variants of Ghomala', Fe'fe', Yemba, Medumba and Kwa.
attributes.government: Traditionally patriarchal and hereditary, under Fons.
attributes.economy: Agriculture is mainly done by women. Bamileke are entrepreneurial, are found in almost all parts of Cameroon, and form much of the business community in coastal towns.

source.citation: WorldAtlas, Ethnic groups of Cameroon, and Wikipedia, Demographics of Cameroon (CC BY-SA 4.0). Compiled for this collection and not yet reviewed by a second person.

attributes.subgroups: Ewondo, Bulu and Fang, with the related Maka, Njem and Baka.
attributes.history: Served as middlemen in the European trade. Some groups were displaced by the Fulani jihad, and the Germans used them for forced labour and road building.
attributes.economy: A strong economic influence through cocoa farming.
attributes.language: Ewondo, the dialect of a Beti clan from the Yaoundé area, has wide currency across the country.

source.citation: Wikipedia, Ethnic groups in Cameroon (CC BY-SA 4.0), and the US State Department background note on Cameroon. Compiled for this collection and not yet reviewed by a second person.

attributes.home: The coastal tropical forest, including Douala, and the Southwest.
attributes.groups: The Duala, the Bassa and many smaller groups, together about 12% of the population in older estimates.
attributes.traditions: The Sawa peoples celebrate the Ngondo festival and wear the kaba ngondo. Makossa originated in Douala, ambasse bey became popular there, and assiko is a Bassa rhythm.
attributes.politics: The nationalist party UPC was based largely among the Bamileke and Bassa.

source.citation: GlobalSecurity.org, Cameroon people, the US State Department background note, and WorldAtlas. Compiled for this collection and not yet reviewed by a second person.

attributes.share: About 14% of the population in older estimates.
attributes.religion: Muslim, with a culture strongly influenced by Islamic practice.
attributes.history: The Fulani conquered most of what is now northern Cameroon between the late 1770s and early 1800s, subjugating or displacing its largely non-Muslim people.
attributes.north: In the Adamawa, North and Far North regions French and Fulfulde are widely spoken.
attributes.title: Rulers in the north are called Lamido.

source.citation: WorldAtlas, Ethnic groups of Cameroon, and Wikipedia, Demographics of Cameroon (CC BY-SA 4.0). Compiled for this collection and not yet reviewed by a second person.

attributes.description: A name for the non-Islamic or recently Islamic peoples of the northern desert and central highlands, about 18% of the population in older estimates.
attributes.origin_of_term: The word was used by outsiders for people who refused to join Islam.
attributes.caution: Treat the term with care, since it comes from outsiders and covers many different peoples.

source.citation: David Zeitlyn's Grassfields research page, Chilver and Kaberry on the kingdom of Kom, and French Wikipedia, Nso (peuple). Compiled for this collection and not yet reviewed by a second person.

attributes.description: A group of peoples whose dynasties founded many Grassfields kingdoms.
attributes.kingdoms: Nso, Kom, Bafut, Bum and Ndu had Tikar or Ndobo-derived dynasties. The Bamum founder Nshare Yèn is called a Tikar prince.
attributes.size: The largest of three groups in one Grassfields study, about 60% of the population there.
attributes.nso: One reference considers the Nso a subgroup of the Tikar.
